title: Programming Techniques & Computational Thinking — Depth Practice
subject: cs

questions.prompt: What must every recursive subroutine have to be guaranteed to terminate?
options: A loop inside the recursive call
A base case that is eventually reached
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — a base case (terminating condition) that the recursive calls progress towards is essential.
questions.feedbackWrong: Recursion terminates only if there is a base case the calls eventually reach; otherwise the stack grows until it overflows.

mistakes.misconception: Believes tracking depth prevents infinite recursion.
mistakes.correction: Depth tracking does nothing unless it is used to stop the recursion — the stopping condition itself is the base case.

questions.prompt:
Trace this algorithm and complete the table for inputs x and output:
```
x ← 12
output ← 0
while x > 0
  output ← output + x
  x ← x − 5
endwhile
```
questions.guidance: Record the values AFTER each loop iteration completes.

questions.prompt: Which data type is most appropriate for storing a person's exact bank balance?
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — balances have fractional parts (pence/cents) so a real type is needed. (In practice decimal fixed-point types are preferred to avoid binary rounding.)
questions.feedbackWrong: A balance like £102.47 has a fractional part — integers can't hold it, strings can't be used in arithmetic, and booleans hold only true/false.

mistakes.correction: Countable in whole pounds only — pence are fractional, and integer division of money loses the remainder.

questions.prompt: Define abstraction in computational thinking, and give one example of how abstraction is used when designing a program to simulate traffic flow through a junction.
questions.guidance: Think about what details a traffic simulation deliberately leaves out.

markScheme.text: Abstraction is removing/hiding unnecessary detail while keeping the features relevant to the problem.
It allows a complex real-world system to be modelled or solved computationally.
Example identifies a relevant feature kept — e.g. number of vehicles, light timings, queue lengths.
Example identifies a detail omitted — e.g. vehicle colour, driver behaviour, weather — as irrelevant to flow rates.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of declaring a variable inside a function rather than outside all functions?
options: It becomes global and visible everywhere
It is local — accessible only within that function
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — variables declared inside a function are local to it, preventing unintended side effects elsewhere.
questions.feedbackWrong: Declaring inside a function creates a local variable, scoped to that function only — this is what protects the rest of the program from side effects.

mistakes.misconception: Reverses the meaning of local and global scope.
mistakes.correction: It is the reverse: variables declared OUTSIDE functions are global; inside, they are local.

questions.prompt: A school wants a program that records student quiz scores, calculates averages per class, and produces a end-of-term report. Explain how decomposition would be applied to designing this system, naming at least three sub-problems.

markScheme.text: Decomposition means breaking a complex problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems.
Sub-problem: input and validation of individual scores.
Sub-problem: storing/retrieving scores in a suitable data structure or file.
Sub-problem: computing class averages from the stored data.
Sub-problem: formatting and outputting the report; notes each sub-problem can be solved/tested independently.

questions.prompt:
Complete the trace table for this algorithm:
```
total ← 0
for i ← 1 to 3
  total ← total + i × 2
next i
```
questions.guidance: One row per loop iteration, values at the end of that iteration.

questions.prompt: The condition `(age >= 18) OR (hasParentalConsent AND age >= 13)` evaluates to true for which case?
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — age 17 fails the first clause but passes both parts of the second: consent AND age ≥ 13.
questions.feedbackWrong: OR requires one side true. The second side needs BOTH consent AND age ≥ 13 — check each option against both clauses.

mistakes.misconception: Ignores the consent requirement in the second clause.
mistakes.correction: AND requires both parts — age 15 with no consent makes the second clause false, and 15 < 18 makes the first false.
